summary: Covered by the dedicated country dossier, which located no Rhineland-Palatine trans statute, hostile-offence series or event-security finding; visitor risk tracks the national framework. The one Land-specific item found is framework-level and resident-facing: a wholly reformed prison-execution code (§ 17 LJ VollzG, in force 1 March 2026) whose new placement rules tie inmate placement to the registry sex entry - part of the wave that made such reforms the majority practice among the 16 Länder, and criticised in a constitutional-law essay as avoidable and in places doubtful.

sources.summary: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (anti-bot 'Access denied' interstitial); per the country dossier this 16 July 2026 France24/wire report covers the neo-Nazi prisoner (the 'Liebich' case) placed in a men's prison despite a legal gender change - the event that drove eastern Länder to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act. Framework-level: prison administration is a Land competence.

Verfassungsblog essay (Clara Wellhäußer, 18 March 2026, 'Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern'): Rhineland-Palatinate's new § 17 LJ VollzG entered into force 1 March 2026 without public attention, completing a majority of Länder that replaced 1970s-era placement rules; all anchor placement to the civil-registry sex entry, though the author argues self-declaration would be a less intrusive, constitutionally safer standard and some new differenzierte rules are doubtful. Resident-detention analysis.

DW report (23 August 2023) on trans inmates in German prisons (the Penelope Frank case): the prison-staff union reports men's prisons inadequately prepared and understaffed (~2,000 officer shortage; ~60,000 inmates in nearly 200 facilities); prisons are Länder jurisdiction and gender-segregation rules bar shared facilities; some states run special facilities or guidelines. National framework context.

localsOnly: The reformed § 17 prison-placement rule and registry-office administration of the self-determination law bind detainees and residents of this Land, not visitors.
